# 21. Tôi nghĩ đây mới là "linh hồn" của Axiom

Nếu gom toàn bộ những gì chúng ta đã thảo luận thành một mô hình:

```text
                   AXIOM
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       │             │             │
      VALUE       OWNERSHIP      TRAIT
       │             │             │
       │          LIFETIME       GENERIC
       │             │             │
       └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                     │
                  SAFETY
                     │
          ┌──────────┴──────────┐
          │                     │
       SAFE CODE             UNSAFE
          │                     │
     native fast             raw power
          │                     │
          └──────────┬──────────┘
                     │
                  MIR/LIR
                     │
              ┌──────┼──────┐
              ▼      ▼      ▼
             x64    ARM64   RISC-V
```

Điểm đặc biệt là:

> **Axiom không cố làm compiler thông minh bằng cách làm language phức tạp.**

Ngược lại:

> **Axiom giữ source semantics đơn giản, rồi để compiler làm phần phức tạp.**

Đây chính là hướng phù hợp với mục tiêu ban đầu của bạn: **người lập trình không phải vật lộn với pointer/lifetime/thread/async, nhưng compiler vẫn tạo ra native code có hiệu năng gần với mức mà một compiler C/C++ tốt có thể đạt được.**

Bước tiếp theo hợp lý nhất là tôi viết tiếp **spec normative thực sự** cho 4 phần này, bắt đầu bằng **`AXIOM-MEMORY-MODEL-v0.1.md`**, trong đó định nghĩa cụ thể **Copy/Move/Drop/View/Alias/Escape/Stack/Heap/Shared Ownership/Unsafe** bằng `MUST / MUST NOT / SHOULD / MAY` và đưa ra khoảng 30–50 test case mà compiler Axiom bắt buộc phải pass.
tiếp tục

Được. Tôi sẽ đi tiếp theo hướng **đóng spec thật sự**, không chỉ mô tả ý tưởng. Phần cần khóa đầu tiên là **Memory Model**, vì Type System, Concurrency và MIR đều phụ thuộc nó.

# AXIOM MEMORY MODEL v0.1

**Status:** FROZEN  
**Layer:** Language Semantics  
**Depends on:** Axiom Core v0.1  
**Used by:** Type System, Concurrency Model, Compiler IR

---

## 1. Memory philosophy

Axiom sử dụng mô hình:

> **Value semantics + ownership semantics + compiler-managed lifetime + explicit unsafe memory access.**

Axiom **không** sử dụng làm mặc định:

- tracing GC
- implicit reference counting
- mandatory object header
- mandatory heap allocation
- mandatory runtime
- programmer-written lifetime annotations
- programmer-written borrow annotations

Mục tiêu:

```text
Simple source
     ↓
Compiler proves lifetime/safety
     ↓
Deterministic native code
```

---

# 2. Storage không phải là Type

Một type không được mặc định gắn với:

```text
stack
heap
register
static
```

Ví dụ:

```axiom
struct Point {
    x: f32
    y: f32
}
```

Compiler có thể đặt `Point`:

```text
register
stack
inline inside another object
heap
static memory
```

miễn semantics không thay đổi.

### MM-001

> Storage location MUST NOT be observable by safe Axiom code, ngoại trừ các API/system operation được khai báo rõ là phụ thuộc storage/address.

---

# 3. Value

Mọi giá trị thông thường là một **value**.

```axiom
let a = 42
let b = a
```

`a` và `b` có semantic identity độc lập.

Compiler có thể tối ưu:

```text
a → register R1
b → register R1
```

nhưng điều này không biến chúng thành alias.

### MM-002

> Copying a value MUST NOT implicitly create shared mutable aliasing.

---

# 4. Copy

Một type có property `Copy` nếu việc sao chép nó không tạo ra hai ownership obligation độc lập.

Ví dụ:

```text
i32
f32
bool
```

là `Copy`.

Một struct chỉ chứa các field `Copy` có thể tự động trở thành `Copy`.

Ví dụ:

```axiom
struct Point {
    x: f32
    y: f32
}
```

có thể:

```text
Point : Copy
```

---

# 5. Move

Owning value có thể được move.

```axiom
let a = Buffer(...)
let b = a
```

semantic:

```text
a ──ownership──> resource

        move

b ──ownership──> resource
a ──invalid─────>
```

Sau move:

```axiom
use(a)
```

là compile error.

### MM-003

> A moved value MUST NOT be used as a valid value after the move.

---

# 6. Move không nhất thiết tạo machine-level copy

Ví dụ:

```axiom
let b = a
```

không có nghĩa compiler phải thực hiện:

```asm
memcpy(...)
```

Move có thể chỉ là:

```text
ownership state:
a → invalid
b → valid
```

Nếu resource đã nằm ở register/stack, compiler có thể chỉ đổi ownership metadata.

---

# 7. Drop

Type có resource lifetime có thể có `Drop`.

Ví dụ:

```axiom
let file = File.open(...)
```

khi lifetime kết thúc:

```text
drop(file)
```

được thực hiện.

### MM-004

> Axiom MUST provide deterministic resource release for owning values.

Nhưng:

> `drop` không đồng nghĩa `free`.

Một `Drop` có thể:

```text
close file
release lock
release GPU resource
return object to pool
decrement explicit shared counter
do nothing
```

---

# 8. Drop elaboration

Source:

```axiom
fn foo() {
    let a = ResourceA()
    let b = ResourceB()

    work()
}
```

MIR có thể trở thành:

```text
BB0:
    a = create ResourceA
    b = create ResourceB

    call work()

    drop b
    drop a

    return
```

Thứ tự mặc định:

> **Reverse declaration order.**

Tương tự nguyên tắc stack unwinding nhưng **không cần exception system**.

---

# 9. Early return

```axiom
fn foo() -> Result {
    let a = ResourceA()

    if condition {
        return error
    }

    ...
}
```

Compiler phải đảm bảo:

```text
condition
   ↓
drop(a)
   ↓
return error
```

Không được leak resource trong safe code.

---

# 10. Panic/trap

Nếu Axiom có:

```axiom
panic(...)
```

compiler phải xác định profile của chương trình.

Có thể có:

```text
panic = terminate
panic = unwind
panic = custom handler
```

Nhưng Memory Model phải đảm bảo rằng **nếu profile sử dụng unwinding**, owning resources vẫn được xử lý đúng.

---

# 11. View

Đây là abstraction quan trọng nhất để giảm pointer/reference syntax.

Conceptually:

```text
view<T>
```

là:

```text
address + extent
```

nhưng:

- không sở hữu data
- không được destroy data
- không được outlive owner
- compiler kiểm tra lifetime

Ví dụ:

```axiom
fn sum(v: view<i32>) -> i32
```

---

# 12. Mutable View

Conceptually:

```text
mut_view<T>
```

cho phép mutation.

```axiom
fn fill(v: mut_view<i32>, value: i32)
```

Trong safe code:

```text
many view<T>
```

được phép cùng tồn tại.

Nhưng:

```text
mut_view<T>
```

không được đồng thời conflict với access khác.

---

# 13. View không phải object

Một view không cần:

```text
refcount
GC metadata
type ID
vtable
object header
```

Nó có thể chỉ là:

```text
(pointer, length)
```

hoặc representation tối ưu khác.

---

# 14. Lifetime của View

Ví dụ:

```axiom
fn get_view() -> view<i32> {
    let data = [1, 2, 3]
    return data
}
```

Nếu `data` là local storage, compiler phải reject:

```text
view escapes owner lifetime
```

Đây là compile-time error.

Không cần programmer viết lifetime annotation.

---

# 15. Escape analysis

Compiler phải theo dõi:

```text
local
 ↓
view
 ↓
return?
store?
global?
spawn?
closure?
```

Nếu lifetime không đủ:

```text
compile error
```

Nếu compiler chứng minh được an toàn:

```text
allow
```

---

# 16. Ownership graph

Compiler có thể nội bộ xây:

```text
Owner A
 │
 ├── View B
 │
 ├── View C
 │
 └── Owned D
```

Nhưng graph này **không phải runtime object**.

Đây là compiler analysis.

---

# 17. Shared ownership

Axiom Core cho phép shared ownership, nhưng Memory Model v0.1 quy định:

> Shared ownership MUST be explicit at the type level.

Ví dụ tương lai:

```text
Shared<T>
AtomicShared<T>
```

Không được:

```axiom
let a = Object()
let b = a
```

vô tình biến thành reference-counted object.

---

# 18. Reference counting

Reference counting **không phải memory primitive của Axiom**.

Có thể triển khai:

```text
Rc<T>
Arc<T>
```

ở library.

Ví dụ:

```text
Rc<T>
 ├── pointer
 └── counter
```

`Arc<T>`:

```text
pointer
atomic counter
```

Nhưng Axiom compiler không tự thêm chúng.

---

# 19. Aliasing

Safe Axiom có ba trạng thái access chính:

```text
READ
WRITE
OWN
```

Quy tắc:

```text
READ + READ      OK
READ + WRITE     conflict
WRITE + WRITE    conflict
OWN + anything   depends on transfer
```

Compiler phải phát hiện conflict.

---

# 20. Nhưng không biến nó thành Rust syntax

Source không cần:

```rust
&T
&mut T
'a
```

Axiom source chủ yếu sử dụng:

```text
T
view<T>
mut_view<T>
```

Compiler có thể có internal concepts tương đương borrow checking.

---

# 21. Unsafe boundary

Raw pointer chỉ được thao tác trong:

```axiom
unsafe { ... }
```

hoặc:

```axiom
unsafe fn ...
```

Ví dụ conceptually:

```axiom
unsafe fn read_memory(addr: usize) -> u32 {
    ...
}
```

Safe code không được tự do:

```text
pointer arithmetic
arbitrary cast
raw memory access
MMIO
volatile access
```

---

# 22. Unsafe không làm compiler bỏ kiểm tra mọi thứ

`unsafe` nghĩa:

> Programmer nhận trách nhiệm đối với invariant mà compiler không thể chứng minh.

Không có nghĩa:

```text
unsafe = compiler off
```

Compiler vẫn kiểm tra:

- syntax
- types
- ABI
- instruction validity
- register constraints
- calling convention

---

# 23. Pointer

Axiom vẫn hỗ trợ:

```text
*const T
*mut T
```

nhưng đây là **low-level representation**.

Không nên để pointer trở thành abstraction chính của application code.

---

# 24. Null

Safe Axiom không có nullable pointer mặc định.

Thay vào đó:

```axiom
Option<T>
```

Ví dụ:

```axiom
fn find(...) -> Option<Item>
```

Raw null pointer chỉ hợp lệ trong:

```text
unsafe
FFI
platform ABI
```

---

# 25. Allocation

Memory Model không quy định allocator cụ thể.

Có thể có:

```text
Global allocator
Arena
Pool
Slab
Stack allocator
Custom allocator
OS allocator
GPU allocator
```

Core chỉ quy định semantic:

```text
allocate
owns
use
release
```

---

# 26. Allocation elimination

Compiler SHOULD thực hiện:

```text
escape analysis
stack promotion
scalar replacement
allocation elimination
```

Ví dụ:

```axiom
fn f() -> Point {
    let p = Point(1, 2)
    return p
}
```

không được mặc định hiểu là:

```text
malloc Point
copy Point
free Point
```

---

# 27. Memory safety invariant

### MM-005

Safe Axiom MUST prevent:

```text
use-after-free
double destruction
dangling view
invalid ownership transfer
data race
out-of-bounds memory access
invalid object lifetime access
```

nếu các hành vi đó không nằm trong explicit unsafe/FFI boundary.

---

# 28. Nhưng không hứa "mọi bug đều bị bắt"

Axiom không được tuyên bố:

> "Memory safe = không thể có memory bug."

Unsafe code, FFI, hardware, compiler bugs, external libraries vẫn có thể phá invariant.

Đúng hơn:

> **Safe Axiom programs do not rely on memory-unsafe behavior.**

---

# 29. Concurrency consequence

Từ Memory Model, ta có:

```text
Owned value
     │
     ├── same thread → normal use
     │
     └── another thread
              │
              ▼
            Send
              │
              ▼
        ownership transfer
```

Shared data:

```text
Shared read
    │
    ├── Thread A
    ├── Thread B
    └── Thread C
```

Mutable shared data:

```text
Mutex
RwLock
Atomic
Channel
```

---

# 30. Test suite tối thiểu

Đây là phần rất quan trọng cho AI agent.

Memory Model không chỉ là document. Nó phải có **executable semantic tests**.

Ví dụ:

### `move_001.ax`

```axiom
fn main() {
    let a = Resource()
    let b = a
    use(a)
}
```

Expected:

```text
COMPILE_ERROR
USE_AFTER_MOVE
```

---

### `copy_001.ax`

```axiom
fn main() {
    let a: i32 = 10
    let b = a

    print(a)
    print(b)
}
```

Expected:

```text
COMPILE_SUCCESS
```

---

### `view_001.ax`

```axiom
fn sum(v: view<i32>) -> i32 {
    ...
}

fn main() {
    let a = [1, 2, 3]
    sum(a)
}
```

Expected:

```text
COMPILE_SUCCESS
```

---

### `view_escape_001.ax`

```axiom
fn get() -> view<i32> {
    let a = [1, 2, 3]
    return a
}
```

Expected:

```text
COMPILE_ERROR
VIEW_OUTLIVES_OWNER
```

---

### `double_drop_001.ax`

```axiom
fn main() {
    let a = Resource()
    let b = a
    drop(a)
}
```

Expected:

```text
COMPILE_ERROR
USE_AFTER_MOVE
```

---

### `send_001.ax`

```axiom
fn main() {
    let data = Buffer(...)

    spawn {
        process(data)
    }
}
```

Nếu `Buffer : Send`:

```text
COMPILE_SUCCESS
```

và ownership chuyển sang task.

---

### `race_001.ax`

Conceptually:

```text
Thread A → write x
Thread B → write x
```

không synchronization.

Expected:

```text
COMPILE_ERROR
DATA_RACE
```

---

# 31. Một vấn đề lớn cần quyết định trước khi đóng Memory Model

Có một câu hỏi tôi **không muốn tự ý quyết định thay bạn**:

## Axiom có nên cho phép implicit temporary views không?

Ví dụ:

```axiom
fn process(v: view<i32>)

fn main() {
    process([1, 2, 3])
}
```

Có hai hướng.

### Hướng A — cho phép

Compiler tạo temporary:

```text
temporary array
     ↓
view
     ↓
process
     ↓
destroy temporary
```

Syntax cực kỳ gọn.

### Hướng B — bắt buộc value phải tồn tại

```axiom
let data = [1, 2, 3]
process(data)
```

Semantic dễ kiểm soát hơn.

**Tôi nghiêng về A**, vì compiler có thể quản lý temporary lifetime hoàn toàn deterministic và tối ưu allocation đi. Nhưng đây là một quyết định semantic đáng để khóa riêng.

---

# 32. Một quyết định thứ hai: `view<T>` có nên là type thật?

Có hai thiết kế:

```text
Axiom source:
view<T>
```

hoặc:

```text
Axiom source:
T
```

và compiler tự suy ra parameter là borrowed/view access dựa trên context.

Tôi hiện **nghiêng về việc có `view<T>`**.

Lý do:

```text
fn process(data: Buffer)
```

rõ ràng:

> Tôi nhận ownership.

Trong khi:

```text
fn process(data: view<Buffer>)
```

rõ ràng:

> Tôi chỉ xem data.

Điều này làm API rất dễ đọc mà không cần Rust lifetime syntax.

---

# 33. Type System sau khi Memory Model khóa

Ta sẽ có một hệ thống rất đẹp:

```text
                         TYPE
                           │
        ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
        │                  │                  │
      VALUE             VIEW             FUNCTION
        │                  │                  │
      Copy/Move       view<T>           closure
        │             mut_view<T>          │
        │                  │               │
      Drop               lifetime        capture
        │                  │               │
        └──────────────────┼───────────────┘
                           │
                       TRAITS
                           │
             ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
             │             │             │
           Copy          Send          Share
             │             │             │
             └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                           │
                     COMPILER ANALYSIS
```

Đây là cơ sở để viết **Type System v0.1** tiếp theo.

---

## Nhưng có một thay đổi kiến trúc tôi đề nghị

Trước khi chuyển sang Type System, tôi muốn **khóa Memory Model thành 3 lớp**, thay vì để tất cả ownership rules nằm cùng một tầng:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Axiom Safe Memory           │
│                                     │
│ Value / Copy / Move / View / Drop   │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│       Axiom Concurrent Memory       │
│                                     │
│ Send / Share / Atomic / Sync        │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│        Axiom Unsafe Memory          │
│                                     │
│ Pointer / Address / FFI / MMIO      │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Như vậy application programmer gần như chỉ sống ở **Safe Memory**, systems programmer có thể xuống **Unsafe Memory**, còn compiler có thể tối ưu xuyên suốt cả ba.

**Bước kế tiếp nên là `Axiom Type System v0.1`**, nhưng lần này tôi sẽ đi sâu vào phần khó nhất: **type properties, generic, trait resolution, `Copy/Move/Drop/Send/Share`, overload, method resolution, type inference và cách tránh "trait hell" của Rust/C++**. Đây là chỗ quyết định Axiom có thực sự đơn giản hơn các ngôn ngữ hiện đại hay không.

Được. Bản này nên đặc biệt tránh một lỗi rất dễ xảy ra: **biến trait thành “class interface + vtable” trá hình**. Tôi sẽ giữ Axiom theo hướng `struct + function + trait + generic constraint`, với static dispatch là mặc định và dynamic dispatch là cơ chế explicit.

# AXIOM CORE TYPE & TRAIT MODEL v0.1

**Status:** FROZEN  
**Edition:** 0.1  
**Layer:** Core Type & Trait System  
**Depends on:**  
- AXIOM CORE SPECIFICATION v0.1
- AXIOM CORE SEMANTIC MODEL v0.1

**Purpose:** Define Axiom's type system, structs, enums, traits, generic constraints, method model, dispatch model, type properties, type composition, and type-level resource semantics.

---

# 1. Purpose

Axiom Core Type & Trait Model defines how types describe:

- values;
- resources;
- behavior;
- capabilities;
- generic constraints;
- ownership properties;
- compile-time dispatch;
- optional runtime dispatch;
- representation;
- ABI behavior.

The model intentionally avoids making traditional object-oriented classes the fundamental abstraction.

Axiom's primary abstraction model is:

```text
TYPE
  │
  ├── DATA ─────────────► struct / enum
  │
  ├── BEHAVIOR ─────────► function
  │
  ├── CONTRACT ─────────► trait
  │
  └── GENERICITY ───────► type parameter + constraint
```

The core principle is:

> **Data and behavior are related by semantic contracts, not by mandatory inheritance hierarchies.**

---

# 2. Fundamental Type Categories

Axiom Core recognizes:

1. Primitive types
2. Struct types
3. Enum types
4. Tuple types
5. Array types
6. Slice/view types
7. Function types
8. Closure types
9. Trait types
10. Generic types
11. Type aliases
12. Reference/view types
13. Pointer types
14. Type-erased/dynamic types
15. Never type

These categories may have different syntax, but they share one static type system.

---

# 3. Static Type System

Axiom is statically typed.

Every expression has a compile-time type.

The compiler must determine:

```text
expression
    ↓
static type
    ↓
valid operations
    ↓
representation
```

before native code generation.

Runtime type information is not required unless the program explicitly requests functionality requiring it.

---

# 4. No Implicit Dynamic Typing

Axiom Core does not define a universal dynamic type similar to:

```text
object
dynamic
any
```

as the default representation.

If a program requires runtime type erasure or dynamic values, it must explicitly use an appropriate mechanism.

This prevents accidental:

- heap allocation;
- runtime type metadata;
- dynamic dispatch;
- boxing.

---

# 5. Primitive Types

The initial Core primitive set is:

```text
i8
i16
i32
i64
i128

u8
u16
u32
u64
u128

f32
f64

bool
char
byte

isize
usize
```

Additional machine-specific primitive types may exist outside the minimal semantic set.

---

# 6. Integer Type Semantics

Integer types have explicit width and signedness.

For example:

```text
i32
u32
```

are distinct types.

Implicit conversion between unrelated integer widths or signedness should not silently change program meaning.

Explicit conversion is preferred.

---

# 7. Integer Overflow

Core distinguishes:

```text
checked arithmetic
wrapping arithmetic
saturating arithmetic
unchecked arithmetic
```

The default safe behavior must be deterministic.

Axiom must not depend on C-style signed-overflow undefined behavior for ordinary arithmetic.

Exact syntax is intentionally left open.

---

# 8. Floating-Point Types

`f32` and `f64` follow the target's specified IEEE-compatible floating-point semantics.

Floating-point behavior may be affected by explicit compiler modes such as fast-math.

Fast-math behavior must never be silently assumed by ordinary safe code.

---

# 9. Bool

`bool` represents exactly two semantic states:

```text
true
false
```

It is not implicitly equivalent to an arbitrary integer.

---

# 10. Byte and Char

`byte` represents an 8-bit unit.

`char` represents a Unicode scalar value according to the language's Unicode model.

Axiom distinguishes:

```text
text
```

from:

```text
raw bytes
```

to prevent accidental confusion between encoded text and binary data.

---

# 11. `usize` and `isize`

`usize` and `isize` are pointer-sized integer types.

They are intended for:

- collection indexes;
- memory sizes;
- offsets;
- platform-sized values;
- interoperability with native APIs.

Their width follows the target ABI.

---

# 12. Structs

Structs are Axiom's primary aggregate data type.

Example:

```axiom
struct Point {
    x: f64
    y: f64
}
```

A struct:

- has a statically known layout unless explicitly dynamic;
- does not inherently allocate on the heap;
- does not inherently have an object header;
- does not inherently have a vtable;
- participates directly in ownership semantics.

---

# 13. Struct Value Semantics

Structs are values by default.

Therefore:

```axiom
let a = Point{1, 2}
let b = a
```

does not imply object identity.

Whether this operation means:

```text
copy
```

or:

```text
move
```

depends on the type's semantic properties and context.

---

# 14. Struct Identity

A struct does not automatically have identity independent of its value.

If identity is required, it must be represented explicitly through an appropriate type/resource.

Examples:

```text
FileHandle
ObjectId
Handle<T>
Arc<T>
```

Identity is therefore not a hidden property of every struct.

---

# 15. Struct Methods

Axiom uses functions with an explicit receiver concept.

Conceptually:

```axiom
fn length(self: String) -> usize
```

may be invoked as:

```axiom
text.length()
```

The receiver is semantically an ordinary parameter.

Therefore:

```text
method
```

is primarily a syntactic convenience over:

```text
function + receiver parameter
```

This preserves a simple core model.

---

# 16. Receiver Modes

A receiver may conceptually be:

```text
owned
immutable
mutable
```

For example:

```text
self
borrowed self
mutable self
```

The exact source syntax is not frozen in this version.

The semantic ownership rules come from CORE SEMANTIC MODEL v0.1.

---

# 17. Extension Methods

A function may operate on a type even if the function is not declared together with the type.

Conceptually:

```axiom
fn area(self: Rectangle) -> f64 {
    ...
}
```

may be usable as:

```axiom
rect.area()
```

This permits modular extension without inheritance.

---

# 18. Method Resolution

Method resolution follows deterministic static rules.

Given:

```text
value.method(args...)
```

the compiler conceptually performs:

```text
receiver type
     ↓
candidate functions
     ↓
visibility
     ↓
receiver compatibility
     ↓
generic constraints
     ↓
trait implementations
     ↓
overload resolution
     ↓
selected function
```

The result must be deterministic.

---

# 19. No Implicit Runtime Method Lookup

Ordinary method calls do not require:

```text
runtime class lookup
reflection
object header
vtable
```

when the target function can be determined statically.

The compiler should lower:

```text
x.method()
```

to a direct function call whenever semantics permit.

---

# 20. Enums

Enums represent a finite set of variants.

Example:

```axiom
enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T)
    Err(E)
}
```

An enum may contain data in its variants.

The compiler determines the most efficient representation consistent with ABI and semantics.

---

# 21. Enum Representation

An enum may conceptually contain:

```text
discriminant
+
variant payload
```

but the compiler may optimize the representation.

Possible optimizations include:

- niche representation;
- pointer tagging;
- integer encoding;
- payload overlay;
- representation compression.

No specific physical layout is required unless ABI representation is explicitly fixed.

---

# 22. Pattern Matching

Pattern matching is type-driven.

The compiler validates:

- variant existence;
- field structure;
- exhaustiveness where required;
- ownership behavior;
- unreachable patterns.

Matching must integrate with ownership semantics.

---

# 23. Option

`Option<T>` represents:

```text
Some(T)
None
```

It is a semantic type, not necessarily a heap object.

The compiler may use optimized representations.

For example, where the representation permits it:

```text
Option<Pointer>
```

may use a null/niche representation without additional storage.

---

# 24. Result

`Result<T, E>` represents:

```text
Ok(T)
Err(E)
```

Ownership follows the active variant.

If:

```text
Result<File, Error>
```

contains `File`, the `File` remains owned by the active `Ok` value.

Moving the `Result` moves the active resource.

---

# 25. Tuple Types

Axiom supports tuple types for compact structural composition.

Example:

```axiom
(i32, f64, bool)
```

Tuples follow ordinary value, ownership, copy, move, and layout semantics.

---

# 26. Arrays

Fixed-size arrays are value types.

Conceptually:

```text
[T; N]
```

represents exactly `N` elements.

The size is part of the type.

Arrays do not inherently require heap allocation.

---

# 27. Slices

A slice is a non-owning view over a sequence.

Conceptually:

```text
slice<T>
    =
pointer/reference
+
length
```

A slice does not own its underlying storage.

Its lifetime cannot exceed the lifetime of the underlying storage.

---

# 28. Dynamic Collections

Dynamic collections such as vectors are library-level types.

For example:

```text
Vector<T>
```

may own:

```text
pointer
length
capacity
allocator
```

but this representation is not part of Core semantics.

The collection's ownership behavior is part of its type contract.

---

# 29. Function Types

Functions are first-class values.

Conceptually:

```text
fn(A, B) -> C
```

represents a callable operation.

A function value may be:

- copied;
- stored;
- passed;
- returned;

according to its type and ABI.

---

# 30. Closure Types

Closures are distinct callable values that may capture environment.

Conceptually:

```text
Closure<F, Environment>
```

but this representation is compiler-internal.

The compiler may erase the environment when it can prove no capture exists.

---

# 31. Function Pointer vs Closure

Axiom distinguishes:

```text
function pointer
```

from:

```text
closure
```

semantically.

A function pointer refers to executable code without an implicit captured environment.

A closure may contain:

```text
code
+
captured state
```

The compiler may convert a noncapturing closure into a function pointer where ABI-compatible.

---

# 32. Traits

A trait defines a set of semantic capabilities or behavioral requirements.

Example:

```axiom
trait Printable {
    fn print(self)
}
```

A trait does not automatically create:

- a class;
- an object;
- a vtable;
- heap allocation;
- runtime metadata.

A trait is primarily a compile-time contract.

---

# 33. Trait Implementation

A type may implement a trait.

Conceptually:

```axiom
impl Printable for User {
    fn print(self) {
        ...
    }
}
```

The exact syntax may evolve, but the semantic relationship is:

```text
User satisfies Printable
```

---

# 34. Trait as Capability

Traits should preferably express capabilities rather than hierarchy.

Examples:

```text
Copyable
Comparable
Hashable
Iterable
Serializable
Sendable
Shareable
Drop
```

A type may implement multiple independent capabilities.

There is no requirement for a single root object hierarchy.

---

# 35. Multiple Trait Implementation

A type may implement multiple traits.

Example:

```text
User:
    Printable
    Hashable
    Comparable
    Sendable
```

Trait composition does not imply multiple inheritance.

Each trait is an independent semantic contract.

---

# 36. Trait Inheritance

Traits may refine other traits.

Conceptually:

```text
trait AdvancedReader: Reader
```

means:

```text
AdvancedReader requires Reader capabilities
```

This is a contract relationship, not object inheritance.

Trait inheritance should remain limited to capability composition.

---

# 37. Trait Methods

Trait methods may be:

- required methods;
- default implementations;
- associated functions;
- associated types/constants where supported.

A trait implementation must satisfy the required semantic contract.

---

# 38. Default Trait Implementations

A trait may provide a default implementation.

Conceptually:

```axiom
trait Printable {
    fn print(self) {
        ...
    }
}
```

A concrete type may use the default implementation or provide its own implementation.

Resolution is static when the concrete type is known.

---

# 39. Method Override

Axiom does not use class override semantics.

Instead:

```text
trait contract
      │
      ├── default implementation
      │
      └── type implementation
```

A type-specific implementation takes precedence over the trait default when the trait rules select it.

This provides the useful part of "override" without requiring class inheritance.

---

# 40. Trait Conflict

If multiple traits provide methods with the same semantic name/signature, method resolution must detect ambiguity.

The compiler should require explicit disambiguation.

For example conceptually:

```text
TraitA::method(x)
TraitB::method(x)
```

rather than silently selecting one based on declaration order.

---

# 41. Inherent vs Trait Methods

A type may have:

```text
inherent functions
```

and:

```text
trait-provided functions
```

Conceptually:

```text
Type
 ├── inherent methods
 └── trait methods
```

Inherent methods are associated directly with the type.

Trait methods require a valid trait implementation/constraint.

---

# 42. Method Resolution Priority

The initial semantic priority is:

```text
1. Exact inherent method
2. Applicable generic/inherent extension
3. Applicable trait method
4. Explicitly requested dynamic dispatch
```

If multiple equally valid candidates remain, compilation fails rather than choosing arbitrarily.

---

# 43. Generic Types

Axiom supports parametric generic types.

Example:

```axiom
struct Box<T> {
    value: T
}
```

`Box<i32>` and `Box<String>` are distinct specialized semantic types.

---

# 44. Generic Functions

Example:

```axiom
fn identity<T>(value: T) -> T {
    return value
}
```

The compiler verifies operations according to the constraints available for `T`.

A generic function cannot assume arbitrary capabilities that were not established by its constraints.

---

# 45. Generic Constraints

Generic constraints specify required capabilities.

Conceptually:

```axiom
fn sort<T: Comparable>(items: Slice<T>)
```

means:

```text
T must satisfy Comparable
```

The constraint is a compile-time requirement.

It does not automatically introduce dynamic dispatch.

---

# 46. Trait Constraints

A generic parameter may require multiple traits.

Conceptually:

```text
T: Comparable + Hashable + Sendable
```

The compiler verifies all requirements.

This is capability composition rather than inheritance.

---

# 47. Static Generic Dispatch

The default generic implementation strategy is static specialization/monomorphization when beneficial.

Conceptually:

```text
generic function<T>
       │
       ├── T = i32
       │      ↓
       │   specialized implementation
       │
       └── T = String
              ↓
           specialized implementation
```

This permits:

- inlining;
- constant propagation;
- dead-code elimination;
- specialization;
- direct calls.

---

# 48. Generic Code Must Not Require Runtime Type Information

A generic type parameter does not automatically imply:

```text
runtime type descriptor
```

If the generic algorithm can be fully resolved statically, the resulting native code may contain no generic metadata.

---

# 49. Dynamic Dispatch

Dynamic dispatch is an explicit semantic choice.

Conceptually:

```text
Dynamic<Trait>
```

or an equivalent mechanism may represent:

```text
runtime value
+
trait operations
```

The exact syntax is not frozen.

The key rule is:

> **Dynamic dispatch must be explicit.**

---

# 50. Dynamic Trait Representation

A dynamic trait value may conceptually contain:

```text
data pointer/reference
+
dispatch table
```

or:

```text
tag
+
operation table
```

or another equivalent representation.

The physical representation is implementation-defined.

---

# 51. No Implicit Vtable

The existence of a trait does not imply a vtable.

For:

```axiom
fn print<T: Printable>(value: T)
```

the compiler should normally generate direct/static dispatch.

Only an explicitly dynamic representation requires runtime dispatch.

---

# 52. Type Erasure

Axiom may provide explicit type erasure.

Conceptually:

```text
Any<Trait>
```

means:

```text
unknown concrete type
+
known trait capabilities
```

Type erasure may require runtime metadata.

That cost is explicit.

---

# 53. Downcasting

Downcasting from a dynamic/type-erased value to a concrete type is not automatically available for all traits.

If supported, it must rely on explicit runtime type information.

Downcasting should not introduce hidden RTTI into ordinary static types.

---

# 54. Associated Types

Traits may define associated types.

Conceptually:

```axiom
trait Container {
    type Item
}
```

Then:

```text
Container::Item
```

is determined by the implementing type.

Associated types are resolved statically whenever possible.

---

# 55. Associated Constants

Traits may define compile-time associated constants.

Example conceptually:

```text
trait Numeric {
    const ZERO
}
```

The compiler may substitute the concrete constant during specialization.

No runtime lookup is required unless explicitly designed that way.

---

# 56. Associated Functions

Traits may define functions that do not require an instance.

Example:

```text
trait Constructible {
    fn create() -> Self
}
```

These remain statically resolvable when the implementing type is known.

---

# 57. `Self`

Traits and type-associated declarations may refer to the implementing type through a conceptual `Self`.

For:

```text
trait Cloneable
```

`Self` means the concrete implementing type.

`Self` is a compile-time concept, not a universal runtime object reference.

---

# 58. Recursive Types

A type may recursively refer to itself only through a finite-size indirection.

Invalid conceptual form:

```text
struct Node {
    next: Node
}
```

because its size would be infinite.

Valid conceptual forms include:

```text
Node {
    next: Box<Node>
}
```

or:

```text
Node {
    next: Handle<Node>
}
```

or another finite representation.

---

# 59. Type Aliases

A type alias creates another name for an existing type.

Conceptually:

```text
type UserId = u64
```

An alias does not create a new nominal type unless explicitly defined as one.

This distinction is important:

```text
alias ≠ new type
```

---

# 60. Newtypes

Axiom supports nominal wrapper/newtype semantics.

Conceptually:

```text
type UserId = newtype(u64)
```

may create a distinct type.

Therefore:

```text
UserId
```

and:

```text
u64
```

are not automatically interchangeable.

Newtypes provide:

- type safety;
- domain modeling;
- zero-cost wrappers;
- trait specialization;
- ABI control.

---

# 61. Transparent Wrappers

A wrapper may explicitly request ABI-transparent representation.

Conceptually:

```text
repr(transparent)
```

means the wrapper is represented compatibly with its underlying field for ABI purposes.

This is useful for:

- FFI;
- handles;
- strong IDs;
- zero-cost abstractions.

---

# 62. Type Layout

The compiler controls ordinary struct layout unless ABI constraints require otherwise.

The compiler may reorder fields to optimize:

- alignment;
- padding;
- size;
- cache behavior.

If a stable layout is required, explicit representation attributes must be available.

---

# 63. C Representation

Axiom must support an explicit C-compatible representation.

Conceptually:

```text
repr(C)
```

This freezes relevant:

- field ordering;
- alignment;
- padding;
- calling convention;
- enum representation.

This is required for FFI.

---

# 64. Packed Representation

Packed representation may be explicitly requested where required.

It may create:

- unaligned accesses;
- performance penalties;
- target-specific constraints.

Packed representation must therefore be explicit.

---

# 65. Alignment

Types have an alignment requirement.

The compiler may increase alignment explicitly where requested.

Alignment affects:

- layout;
- ABI;
- SIMD;
- atomics;
- hardware access.

---

# 66. Zero-Sized Types

A type may have zero runtime size when it carries no runtime state.

Examples conceptually:

```text
Marker
Phantom<T>
Capability
```

Zero-sized types should impose no storage cost when not otherwise required.

---

# 67. Phantom Type Parameters

A type may contain a generic parameter used only for compile-time semantics.

Conceptually:

```text
Handle<T>
```

where `T` is not physically stored.

The compiler may erase the phantom parameter from runtime representation.

---

# 68. Type-Level Safety

Phantom types and newtypes may encode semantic distinctions such as:

```text
Meters
Seconds
UserId
FileHandle
GpuHandle
Initialized
Uninitialized
```

without runtime overhead when representation permits.

---

# 69. Type Properties

The compiler conceptually tracks intrinsic type properties.

Initial properties include:

```text
Copyable
Movable
Destructible
Sendable
Shareable
Sized
ZeroSized
Trivial
```

Additional properties may be introduced later.

---

# 70. Copyable

A type marked or inferred as `Copyable` may be duplicated without ownership transfer.

Copy semantics must preserve the type's observable meaning.

A resource type with unique external ownership is normally not copyable.

---

# 71. Movable

A type is movable when ownership can be transferred.

Most resource-bearing values should be movable even when they are not copyable.

The conceptual relationship is:

```text
Copyable ⊆ Movable
```

for ordinary value semantics.

A type may have special semantics, but Core should avoid unnecessary exceptions.

---

# 72. Destructible

A type is destructible when its lifetime ending requires resource cleanup.

A trivial integer is normally not meaningfully destructible.

A file handle is.

The compiler may optimize trivial destruction away.

---

# 73. Sendable

`Sendable` represents the ability to transfer a value across execution contexts safely according to Axiom's concurrency model.

Conceptually:

```text
Sendable<T>
```

means ownership of `T` may cross a thread/task boundary under the defined conditions.

---

# 74. Shareable

`Shareable` represents the ability to share a value between execution contexts under its semantic contract.

Immutable values may be naturally shareable.

Mutable values generally require synchronization or an explicitly safe shared abstraction.

---

# 75. Copyability and Sendability

These are independent concepts.

A type can be:

```text
copyable + sendable
```

or:

```text
move-only + sendable
```

For example, a file handle may be movable between threads without being copyable.

---

# 76. Sendable and Raw Pointers

Raw pointers are not automatically considered `Sendable`.

The programmer or API must establish that transferring the pointed-to resource is safe.

This prevents accidental thread transfer of arbitrary memory addresses.

---

# 77. Shareable and Mutable State

A mutable struct is not automatically safely shareable.

For example:

```text
Counter
```

does not become thread-safe merely because it is a struct.

A synchronization abstraction must establish safe sharing.

---

# 78. Trait Derivation

The compiler may derive certain properties automatically when it can prove them.

For example:

```text
struct Point {
    x: i32
    y: i32
}
```

may automatically satisfy:

```text
Copyable
Sendable
Shareable
```

when its fields satisfy the corresponding contracts.

Derivation must be deterministic.

---

# 79. Negative Trait Derivation

A type containing a non-copyable field must not automatically become copyable.

Example:

```text
struct User {
    file: File
}
```

If `File` is not copyable:

```text
Copyable(User) = false
```

unless the type explicitly provides valid custom copy semantics.

---

# 80. Custom Copy Semantics

A type may define custom duplication semantics when meaningful.

However, "copy" must not silently mean "duplicate an externally unique resource."

For example:

```text
File
```

should not become copyable merely because an implementation can duplicate an OS handle.

If duplication has meaningful resource semantics, it should be an explicit operation such as:

```text
clone
duplicate
share
```

rather than implicit copy.

---

# 81. Clone vs Copy

Axiom distinguishes cheap semantic copy from potentially expensive explicit duplication.

Conceptually:

```text
Copy
    = implicit, ordinary value duplication

Clone
    = explicit duplication operation
```

A clone may:

- allocate;
- perform I/O;
- duplicate an OS handle;
- copy a large buffer.

Therefore clone operations should remain explicit.

---

# 82. Drop / Destruction Trait

A type may provide destruction behavior.

The conceptual capability is:

```text
Destructible / Drop
```

The exact trait name is intentionally not frozen.

Destruction is automatically invoked according to ownership/lifetime rules.

---

# 83. Destructor Restrictions

Destruction must not:

- resurrect an invalid owner;
- create ownership ambiguity;
- silently duplicate unique resources;
- violate ABI contracts.

A destructor may perform external cleanup such as:

```text
close file
release socket
free memory
unlock resource
```

according to the type's semantics.

---

# 84. Trait Coherence

Axiom requires deterministic trait resolution.

For a given:

```text
Type + Trait
```

there should be one unambiguous implementation in a compilation environment unless explicit specialization rules permit otherwise.

This avoids unpredictable dispatch.

---

# 85. Orphan Rule Direction

The precise orphan/coherence mechanism remains open, but the Core requires protection against uncontrolled conflicting implementations.

A package should not be able to create arbitrary competing implementations of foreign types and foreign traits without a deterministic resolution model.

---

# 86. Specialization

Generic specialization may be supported.

However, specialization must preserve:

- type soundness;
- deterministic method resolution;
- trait coherence;
- ABI correctness.

Specialization rules are not fully frozen in v0.1.

---

# 87. Overloading

Axiom may support function/method overloading based on statically resolvable signatures.

Overload resolution must be:

- deterministic;
- compile-time;
- unambiguous.

Overloading must not silently become runtime dispatch.

---

# 88. Implicit Conversion

Implicit conversions should be extremely limited.

Safe implicit conversion may be allowed where it cannot silently lose information or radically alter semantics.

Examples that should normally require explicit conversion:

```text
i64 → i32
u64 → i32
f64 → i32
raw pointer → reference
```

This protects predictability.

---

# 89. Numeric Promotion

Arithmetic involving mixed numeric types should follow explicit, deterministic promotion rules.

The compiler must never silently choose a surprising precision or signedness conversion.

Exact promotion tables remain to be frozen separately.

---

# 90. Generic Variance

Axiom Core does not automatically adopt complex variance rules from object-oriented type systems.

For ordinary value types:

```text
T
```

is invariant unless a specific abstraction defines safe variance.

This avoids hidden substitution behavior.

---

# 91. Function Variance

Function types follow normal type-theoretic parameter/result compatibility rules where needed.

The compiler must preserve safety when assigning function values.

Exact variance rules will be defined in the function-type specification.

---

# 92. Trait Objects and Variance

Dynamic trait objects should not inherit arbitrary variance rules.

Their compatibility must be explicitly defined by the trait-object model.

---

# 93. Type Inference

Axiom supports local type inference.

Example:

```axiom
let x = 42
```

The compiler determines the appropriate type.

Inference must remain deterministic.

---

# 94. Inference Does Not Mean Dynamic Typing

The fact that the programmer does not write:

```text
i32
```

does not mean the variable is dynamically typed.

The compiler still establishes a concrete static type.

---

# 95. Public API Type Inference

Public interfaces should expose sufficient explicit type information for stable API semantics.

Axiom may allow inferred implementation details while requiring exported signatures to have compiler-resolvable public types.

---

# 96. Type Equality

Axiom distinguishes:

```text
structural equality
```

from:

```text
nominal identity
```

as appropriate.

Two independently declared nominal structs with identical fields are not automatically the same type.

Example:

```text
Meters
Seconds
```

may both contain `f64` but remain distinct types.

---

# 97. Structural Types

Some types may intentionally use structural identity:

- tuples;
- function types;
- slices;
- arrays.

For these types, shape and constituent types determine compatibility.

---

# 98. Nominal Types

User-defined structs, enums, and newtypes are nominal by default.

This provides strong domain separation.

For example:

```text
UserId
ProductId
```

may both wrap `u64` but cannot be accidentally mixed.

---

# 99. Recursive Generic Constraints

Axiom may support constraints involving the implementing type.

Conceptually:

```text
T: Comparable<T>
```

or:

```text
T: Iterator<Item = T>
```

Such constraints must be resolved statically.

---

# 100. Trait Associated Requirements

A trait may define requirements over associated types.

Conceptually:

```text
trait Iterator {
    type Item
    fn next(self) -> Option<Item>
}
```

Generic algorithms may then operate over:

```text
T: Iterator
```

without knowing the concrete item type until specialization.

---

# 101. Trait Composition

Multiple traits may be combined into a generic requirement.

Conceptually:

```text
T: Readable + Writable + Sendable
```

This means:

```text
T satisfies all three contracts
```

It does not mean:

```text
T inherits three classes
```

---

# 102. Trait Upcasting

Trait-to-supertrait conversion may be supported where semantically valid.

Example:

```text
AdvancedReader
       ↓
Reader
```

The conversion must not accidentally require dynamic allocation when static representation is sufficient.

---

# 103. Trait Implementation Is Not Object Creation

Implementing:

```text
Printable for User
```

does not create a `Printable` object.

It creates a compile-time relationship:

```text
User satisfies Printable
```

Only explicit type erasure/dynamic dispatch creates a runtime trait representation.

---

# 104. Static Dispatch Model

For:

```text
fn print<T: Printable>(x: T)
```

the compiler resolves:

```text
T
 ↓
Printable implementation for T
 ↓
concrete function
```

before native code generation whenever possible.

No vtable is required.

---

# 105. Dynamic Dispatch Model

For an explicitly dynamic value:

```text
dyn Printable
```

the compiler may generate:

```text
data
+
vtable
```

or an equivalent representation.

This is the explicit cost of runtime polymorphism.

---

# 106. Dynamic Dispatch Is an Optimization Boundary

The compiler may devirtualize a dynamic call when it can prove the concrete type.

Therefore:

```text
dynamic semantics
```

do not prevent:

```text
static optimization
```

when semantics permit.

---

# 107. Trait Object Lifetime

A dynamic trait value containing a reference must preserve the referenced object's lifetime.

The trait object cannot outlive its underlying resource.

If the dynamic object owns its data, ownership must be transferred into the dynamic representation.

---

# 108. Trait Object Ownership

A dynamic trait object may be:

```text
borrowed
owned
shared
```

according to its wrapper/type.

This prevents the trait abstraction from implicitly choosing a memory-management model.

---

# 109. Type-Erased Resource Destruction

An owned dynamic value must retain enough information to correctly destroy its concrete resource.

This may require:

```text
destructor function pointer
```

or equivalent metadata.

Such metadata is justified because dynamic ownership explicitly requires it.

---

# 110. No Universal Object Header

Axiom does not require every runtime value to contain:

```text
type ID
vtable
refcount
GC metadata
object header
```

Only abstractions that semantically require such metadata may carry it.

---

# 111. Compile-Time Reflection

Axiom favors compile-time reflection/introspection.

Examples:

```text
fields<T>
methods<T>
size_of<T>
align_of<T>
traits<T>
```

These should preferably resolve during compilation.

Runtime reflection is optional and explicit.

---

# 112. Runtime Type Information

RTTI is not mandatory.

If an application needs:

```text
type identity at runtime
dynamic casting
serialization metadata
plugin discovery
```

the application may explicitly request the required metadata.

Unused RTTI must not appear in ordinary binaries.

---

# 113. Type IDs

If runtime type identification exists, the identifier must be deterministic and ABI-safe.

It must not depend on:

- memory address;
- compilation order;
- random values.

The exact type-ID mechanism remains open.

---

# 114. Compile-Time `size_of`

The compiler must be able to determine the size of statically sized types.

Conceptually:

```text
size_of<T>()
align_of<T>()
```

may be compile-time operations.

For dynamic types, the representation may require runtime information.

---

# 115. Unsized Types

Some abstractions may have dynamically sized representations.

Examples:

```text
str
dyn Trait
dynamic slice representation
```

Such values generally require an associated metadata representation.

The exact unsized-type model remains open.

---

# 116. Ownership + Type System

Ownership properties belong to types.

For example:

```text
File
```

may semantically be:

```text
Moveable
!Copyable
Destructible
Sendable
!Shareable
```

while:

```text
i32
```

may be:

```text
Copyable
Moveable
Trivial
Sendable
Shareable
!Destructible
```

The compiler uses these properties during semantic analysis.

---

# 117. Type Capability Lattice

Conceptually, Axiom may model capabilities as:

```text
                  Type
                   │
        ┌──────────┼───────────┐
        ▼          ▼           ▼
     Copyable   Sendable    Destructible
        │          │
        ▼          ▼
     Movable    Shareable
```

This diagram is conceptual only.

Actual trait relationships must be defined consistently.

---

# 118. Resource Type Example

Conceptually:

```text
File
 ├── Moveable
 ├── Destructible
 ├── Sendable
 ├── !Copyable
 └── !Shareable
```

This means:

```text
File can move
File must eventually be destroyed
File can cross a thread boundary if valid
File cannot be implicitly copied
File cannot be freely shared
```

---

# 119. Value Type Example

Conceptually:

```text
Point
 ├── Copyable
 ├── Moveable
 ├── Sendable
 ├── Shareable
 └── Trivial
```

The compiler may pass `Point` entirely in registers.

---

# 120. Strong Type Example

Conceptually:

```text
type UserId = newtype(u64)
```

The runtime representation may remain:

```text
u64
```

while the compiler prevents:

```text
UserId + ProductId
```

when such an operation is not defined.

This is a zero-cost type-safety mechanism.

---

# 121. Behavior Example

```text
struct Point {
    x: f64
    y: f64
}

fn distance(self: Point, other: Point) -> f64
```

The language does not need:

```text
class Point
virtual method
object header
```

The compiler can generate an ordinary native function.

---

# 122. Trait Example

Conceptually:

```text
trait Printable {
    fn print(self)
}

impl Printable for Point {
    fn print(self) {
        ...
    }
}
```

A generic call:

```text
fn show<T: Printable>(x: T)
```

can compile to a direct `Point` implementation when instantiated with `Point`.

---

# 123. Default Implementation Example

Conceptually:

```text
trait Printable {
    fn print(self) {
        ...
    }
}
```

A type can accept the default implementation.

If it defines its own:

```text
impl Printable for Point {
    fn print(self) {
        ...
    }
}
```

the concrete implementation replaces the default for that type.

---

# 124. Dynamic Trait Example

Conceptually:

```text
let value: dyn Printable = point
```

may require:

```text
data
+
dispatch metadata
```

The programmer explicitly requested runtime polymorphism.

---

# 125. Generic Algorithm Example

Conceptually:

```text
fn sum<T: Add + Zero>(items: Slice<T>) -> T
```

The compiler may specialize:

```text
sum_i32
sum_f64
sum_CustomNumber
```

with direct operations.

No universal runtime generic object is required.

---

# 126. Type System and ABI

The type system must expose enough information to generate stable native ABIs.

For ABI-visible types, the compiler must know:

```text
size
alignment
layout
calling convention
parameter passing
return passing
ownership contract
destruction contract
```

---

# 127. ABI-Sensitive Types

The following should support explicit ABI representation:

```text
struct
enum
newtype
function
trait object
slice
string
```

This is necessary for:

- C interop;
- system libraries;
- plugins;
- shared libraries;
- native applications.

---

# 128. Standard Library Relationship

Core types define semantics.

The standard library provides implementations such as:

```text
String
Vector
HashMap
File
Socket
Mutex
Thread
Channel
Arc
Box
Arena
```

These are not automatically part of the language core.

This separation keeps Core small.

---

# 129. Smart Pointers

Smart-pointer abstractions are library/type-level mechanisms.

Possible examples:

```text
Box<T>
Rc<T>
Arc<T>
Weak<T>
Unique<T>
Handle<T>
```

Core does not require every program to use them.

A smart pointer is simply another type with defined ownership semantics.

---

# 130. Box

A `Box<T>`-like type may represent:

```text
owned heap allocation containing T
```

Semantically:

```text
Box<T>
    owns
      ↓
    T
```

The heap allocation is explicit through the type rather than silently imposed on `T`.

---

# 131. Reference-Counted Types

`Rc<T>` or `Arc<T>` may implement shared ownership.

The cost is explicit:

```text
reference counting
atomic operations
control block
```

Such types are not hidden language behavior.

---

# 132. Arena Handles

A library may define:

```text
Handle<T>
```

where the arena owns actual objects.

This allows:

- stable IDs;
- graph structures;
- entity systems;
- compact storage;
- custom allocation.

The language core remains independent of the arena implementation.

---

# 133. Type Erasure Cost Principle

If a programmer chooses:

```text
dynamic
Any
dyn Trait
type erased container
```

runtime metadata may be required.

The cost is explicit.

If they choose:

```text
generic<T>
```

the compiler should prefer static specialization.

---

# 134. No Hidden Boxing

Passing a value to a generic or trait-based function must not silently allocate a heap object solely to satisfy the abstraction.

Boxing may occur only when the chosen representation explicitly requires it.

---

# 135. No Hidden Virtual Dispatch

Calling:

```text
value.method()
```

must not automatically become a vtable call because the method is declared through a trait.

Static knowledge should be exploited.

---

# 136. No Hidden Reference Counting

Passing or returning an ordinary value must not implicitly increment/decrement reference counts.

Reference counting occurs only for explicit shared-ownership types.

---

# 137. No Hidden Runtime Type Checks

Generic constraints and static trait implementations should be resolved at compile time.

Runtime type checks occur only when explicit dynamic semantics require them.

---

# 138. Type System Safety Boundary

The type system is responsible for establishing:

```text
type correctness
ownership properties
trait satisfaction
generic constraints
representation rules
ABI contracts
```

The optimizer is responsible for:

```text
performance
code size
allocation elimination
dispatch elimination
```

The runtime, when present, is responsible only for services that cannot or should not be statically eliminated.

---

# 139. Compiler Representation

Axiom's semantic type representation should conceptually include:

```text
TypeId
Kind
Size
Alignment
Layout
Ownership properties
Trait implementations
Generic parameters
Associated types
ABI properties
Drop behavior
Send/Share properties
```

This metadata exists primarily in compiler IR.

It does not automatically become binary metadata.

---

# 140. Type Identity

Every named nominal type receives a stable semantic identity within the compiler.

The compiler must distinguish:

```text
ModuleA.User
ModuleB.User
```

even if their fields are identical.

This prevents accidental type collision.

---

# 141. Generic Type Identity

A generic specialization has identity based on:

```text
generic definition
+
type arguments
+
relevant compile-time parameters
```

For example:

```text
Vector<i32>
```

and:

```text
Vector<f64>
```

are distinct semantic specializations.

---

# 142. Module Qualification

Type resolution must respect modules/namespaces.

Conceptually:

```text
graphics.Point
physics.Point
```

are distinct names even if both define `Point`.

Imports may provide shorter aliases.

---

# 143. Visibility

Types and trait implementations may have visibility:

```text
private
module
public
```

Visibility affects semantic accessibility, not memory representation.

---

# 144. Sealed Behavior

A trait may optionally be restricted so external modules cannot implement it.

This can preserve:

- exhaustive reasoning;
- ABI guarantees;
- optimization assumptions;
- coherence.

Exact syntax remains open.

---

# 145. Exhaustive Enums

An enum may be exhaustively matchable when its set of variants is closed and visible.

For externally extensible types, exhaustive matching may not be guaranteed.

The compiler must distinguish these cases.

---

# 146. Open vs Closed Traits

A trait may conceptually be:

```text
open
```

meaning external implementations are allowed, or:

```text
sealed
```

meaning implementations are controlled.

The exact module/package rules remain to be defined.

---

# 147. Trait Object Safety

Not every trait must automatically be usable as a dynamic trait object.

Traits requiring:

- unresolved generic methods;
- certain associated-type behavior;
- static-only operations;

may be incompatible with runtime dynamic representation.

The compiler must diagnose this explicitly.

---

# 148. Static-Only Traits

A trait may intentionally exist only for compile-time generic programming.

Examples:

```text
ConstEvaluable
CompileTimeType
Specializable
```

Such traits never require runtime representation.

---

# 149. Runtime-Capable Traits

A trait intended for dynamic dispatch must have a representation-compatible method set.

The compiler may generate:

```text
vtable
type metadata
destructor metadata
```

only for the dynamic representation.

---

# 150. Trait Object ABI

If dynamic trait values cross an ABI boundary, their representation must be explicitly specified.

Axiom must not expose an unstable internal vtable format as a default FFI ABI.

---

# 151. Type-Level Compile-Time Evaluation

Types and traits may participate in compile-time evaluation where supported.

Examples:

```text
size_of<T>
align_of<T>
trait_satisfied<T, Trait>
```

These should preferably resolve before runtime.

---

# 152. Const Generics

Axiom may support compile-time value parameters.

Conceptually:

```text
Array<T, N>
```

where:

```text
N
```

is a compile-time integer.

This allows:

```text
Array<i32, 16>
```

without runtime size metadata.

Exact syntax remains open.

---

# 153. Generic Value Parameters

Future generic parameters may include:

```text
type
integer
boolean
enum value
compile-time constant
```

The semantic principle is:

> **Compile-time parameters should disappear from runtime representation whenever they are not semantically required.**

---

# 154. Type-Level Arithmetic

If const generics are implemented, compile-time expressions may calculate sizes and constraints.

Example conceptually:

```text
Matrix<T, Rows, Cols>
```

The compiler can calculate:

```text
Rows * Cols
```

at compile time.

---

# 155. Compile-Time Assertions

Types and generic constraints may participate in compile-time assertions.

Examples:

```text
assert size_of<T>() == expected
assert align_of<T>() >= required
assert T: Sendable
```

These must fail compilation when constraints are not satisfied.

---

# 156. Type Safety and Zero Cost

Axiom strongly favors compile-time type distinctions that have no runtime cost.

Examples:

```text
newtype
phantom type
trait constraint
generic specialization
compile-time constant
```

These are preferred over runtime tagging when runtime information is unnecessary.

---

# 157. Runtime Cost Must Follow Semantic Need

The type system follows:

```text
compile-time information
        ↓
should disappear

runtime-required information
        ↓
may remain
```

This principle prevents the type system from becoming a hidden runtime.

---

# 158. Type System and Unsafe

Unsafe code may bypass certain type-system safety guarantees.

However, types remain relevant inside unsafe code for:

- layout;
- ABI;
- alignment;
- ownership contracts;
- destructor semantics.

Unsafe is not an untyped mode.

---

# 159. Raw Pointer Type

A raw pointer is a distinct type from a safe reference.

Conceptually:

```text
*const T
*mut T
```

or equivalent.

Raw pointers:

- may be null;
- may be dangling;
- may be unaligned;
- may not point to valid objects;
- do not automatically imply ownership.

Their use is primarily unsafe.

---

# 160. Pointer Ownership

A raw pointer carries no ownership semantics by itself.

If ownership exists, it must be represented by an explicit type or contract.

Therefore:

```text
*mut T
```

does not mean:

```text
owns T
```

---

# 161. Reference vs Pointer

Semantic distinction:

```text
Reference
    = valid access to an existing value

Raw pointer
    = machine address with minimal guarantees
```

This distinction allows safe code to avoid pointer complexity while retaining low-level capabilities.

---

# 162. Handles

A handle is a value representing access to an external resource.

Example:

```text
Handle<File>
Handle<GPUBuffer>
Handle<Window>
```

Handles are ordinary types and may have explicit ownership semantics.

They are useful when:

- resource identity matters;
- storage is externally managed;
- stable addresses are undesirable;
- arena allocation is used.

---

# 163. Type-Level Ownership Wrappers

Axiom encourages explicit wrappers when ownership semantics differ.

For example:

```text
Borrow<T>
Owned<T>
Shared<T>
Weak<T>
Handle<T>
```

These are conceptually different contracts.

They need not all be built into Core.

---

# 164. Core Type Design Rule

The type system should make it possible to express:

```text
I own this.
I temporarily access this.
I exclusively mutate this.
I share this.
I transfer this.
This can cross threads.
This requires synchronization.
This is only compile-time.
This requires runtime dispatch.
```

without forcing all programs to use all of these mechanisms.

---

# 165. Explicit Cost Model

Axiom's preferred cost model is:

```text
struct
    → no mandatory allocation

trait
    → no mandatory vtable

generic
    → no mandatory runtime metadata

method
    → no mandatory object lookup

closure
    → no mandatory heap allocation

newtype
    → no mandatory runtime overhead

ownership
    → no mandatory runtime ownership metadata

shared ownership
    → explicit cost

dynamic dispatch
    → explicit cost

type erasure
    → explicit cost

heap ownership
    → explicit cost
```

---

# 166. Core Invariants

The following invariants are FROZEN.

### TYPE-001
Every expression has a statically determined type.

### TYPE-002
Structs are primary aggregate values.

### TYPE-003
Structs do not imply heap allocation.

### TYPE-004
Traits are contracts, not mandatory runtime objects.

### TYPE-005
Trait implementation does not imply a vtable.

### TYPE-006
Generic constraints are compile-time by default.

### TYPE-007
Generic specialization does not inherently require runtime metadata.

### TYPE-008
Dynamic dispatch must be explicit.

### TYPE-009
Type erasure must be explicit.

### TYPE-010
Nominal user-defined types are distinct even when structurally identical.

### TYPE-011
Newtypes may provide zero-cost semantic distinctions.

### TYPE-012
Ownership properties belong to types.

### TYPE-013
Copy and move semantics are distinct.

### TYPE-014
Destruction semantics belong to the type/resource contract.

### TYPE-015
Send/share properties are type-level contracts.

### TYPE-016
Raw pointers do not imply ownership.

### TYPE-017
Safe references cannot outlive their targets.

### TYPE-018
ABI-sensitive representations must be explicit.

### TYPE-019
Runtime metadata is emitted only when required.

### TYPE-020
Type abstraction must not inherently impose runtime cost.

---

# 167. Explicitly Rejected From Core v0.1

The following are rejected as default language semantics:

```text
mandatory class inheritance
mandatory object headers
mandatory vtables
mandatory garbage collection
mandatory reference counting
mandatory boxing
mandatory RTTI
mandatory dynamic dispatch
mandatory heap allocation for objects
universal dynamic type
implicit runtime type checks
implicit shared ownership
implicit virtual methods
implicit cloning of resources
```

---

# 168. Core Type Philosophy

Axiom's type system should behave like:

```text
        TYPE
         │
    ┌────┼────┐
    ▼    ▼    ▼
   DATA BEHAVIOR CONTRACT
    │    │    │
    ▼    ▼    ▼
 struct func  trait
    │    │    │
    └────┼────┘
         ▼
       GENERIC
```

rather than:

```text
Object
  │
  ├── Class
  │    ├── Base
  │    ├── Virtual
  │    └── Derived
  │
  └── Runtime Object
       ├── Header
       ├── RTTI
       └── VTable
```

---

# 169. Final Model

The Axiom type system can be summarized as:

```text
TYPE
 │
 ├── VALUE
 │     ├── primitive
 │     ├── struct
 │     ├── enum
 │     ├── tuple
 │     └── array
 │
 ├── VIEW
 │     ├── reference
 │     └── slice
 │
 ├── CALLABLE
 │     ├── function
 │     └── closure
 │
 ├── CONTRACT
 │     └── trait
 │
 ├── PARAMETRIC
 │     └── generic
 │
 ├── IDENTITY
 │     ├── newtype
 │     └── handle
 │
 └── DYNAMIC
       └── explicit type erasure
```

And behavior resolution:

```text
Concrete Type
     │
     ├── inherent function
     │
     ├── generic constraint
     │
     ├── trait implementation
     │
     └── explicit dynamic dispatch
```

with the default path being:

```text
Concrete Type
      ↓
Compile-Time Resolution
      ↓
Direct Native Call
```

not:

```text
Concrete Type
      ↓
Runtime Object
      ↓
VTable
      ↓
Indirect Call
```

---

# 170. Final Design Principle

Axiom Core Type & Trait Model v0.1 is governed by one central principle:

> **A type describes what a value is capable of; a trait describes what a type guarantees; a function describes what can be done; ownership describes who controls lifetime; and dynamic machinery appears only when the programmer explicitly requires runtime polymorphism or runtime state.**

Axiom therefore aims for:

> **Structs instead of mandatory classes.**

> **Traits instead of inheritance hierarchies.**

> **Functions instead of implicit object machinery.**

> **Generics instead of mandatory dynamic polymorphism.**

> **Explicit dynamic dispatch instead of hidden vtables.**

> **Newtypes instead of runtime wrappers.**

> **Compile-time capabilities instead of runtime metadata.**

> **Explicit resource abstractions instead of implicit heap objects.**

---

# 171. Status

**AXIOM CORE TYPE & TRAIT MODEL v0.1 — FROZEN**

Future revisions must explicitly identify:

```text
ADDED
CHANGED
REMOVED
INCOMPATIBLE
```

Any change affecting:

- type identity;
- struct semantics;
- enum representation;
- trait resolution;
- generic constraints;
- method resolution;
- copy/move properties;
- Send/Share properties;
- dynamic dispatch;
- ABI representation;

must be treated as a **Core Type System Change**, not merely a compiler implementation detail.
:::
